rosa-parks.excerpt: She was not a tired seamstress who happened to be in the wrong seat. And her famous arrest photo isn't from that day.
sections: Tuskegee and Montgomery

Rosa Louise McCauley was born in Tuskegee, Alabama, on 4 February 1913. She spent her first years on a small farm with her mother, grandparents and brother, where she saw the Ku Klux Klan ride at night and heard of lynchings nearby. The family moved to Montgomery; she went to school there, became a seamstress, and in 1932 married Raymond Parks, a barber active in the NAACP. She finished high school the next year.
Twelve years an activist

In 1943 Parks joined the Montgomery NAACP and was elected its secretary, a post she held for twelve years. She founded its youth council, and as secretary of the state NAACP she travelled to interview victims of discrimination and witnesses to lynchings. In the summer of 1955 she attended a workshop on social justice at the Highlander Folk School in Tennessee. She had defied bus segregation before; in 1943 a driver, James Blake, had put her off his bus for refusing to re-board by the back door. "I never wanted to be on that man's bus again," she wrote, and she avoided it for twelve years.
Nine months before her own arrest, a fifteen-year-old, Claudette Colvin, was arrested for refusing to give up her seat. Parks helped raise money for her defence.
1 December 1955

On the evening of 1 December 1955, Parks boarded bus 2857 without noticing who was driving: James Blake. She took a seat in the first row of the section open to Black passengers. When a white man was left standing, Blake ordered her and three others to move. Only Parks refused. She was arrested, and on 5 December she was convicted of disorderly conduct and breaking the city ordinance. In her autobiography she dismissed the story that she was simply tired: the only tired she was, she wrote, was tired of giving in.
381 days

On the day of her trial, 5 December, Black Montgomery stayed off the buses. The boycott lasted 381 days; some 17,000 people took part, and Parks served on the executive board of the organising group and worked as a dispatcher for its car pools. On 21 February 1956 a grand jury indicted her and more than a hundred others under an old anti-boycott law, and she was arrested again. The next day, 22 February 1956, she was photographed being fingerprinted. That is the picture most people know. It is often shown as if it came from 1 December 1955; it was taken almost three months later. The date comes from the Smithsonian's National Portrait Gallery and the Library of Congress.
In 1956, in Browder v. Gayle, a case brought by four other women including Colvin, the Supreme Court ruled Montgomery's bus segregation unconstitutional. The boycott ended on 21 December 1956.
Detroit

Her stand came at a cost. Parks lost her job at a department store, her husband quit his, and they received death threats. In 1957 they moved to Detroit, where from 1965 to 1988 she worked for Congressman John Conyers. She founded a scholarship foundation in 1980 and, with her husband's memory, the Rosa and Raymond Parks Institute for Self-Development in 1987, and published her autobiography in 1992. Congress awarded her its Gold Medal in 1999.

Rosa Parks died in Detroit on 24 October 2005, at 92. She became the first woman to lie in honor in the Rotunda of the United States Capitol; more than 30,000 people filed past. In 2013 a statue of her was unveiled in the Capitol, the first full-length statue of an African American there. One seat. 381 days. A country changed.

sojourner-truth.excerpt: In 1828 a formerly enslaved mother went to court in New York against the man who had sold her son illegally. And she won.
sections: Isabella

She was born into slavery in Ulster County, New York, around 1797, to James and Elizabeth Baumfree, and named Isabella. Her first language was Dutch. At about nine she was sold away from her parents, with a flock of sheep, for a hundred dollars; by 1810 she belonged to John Dumont of West Park, and stayed his property for sixteen years. There she was abused by both Dumonts. Around 1815 she fell in love with Robert, an enslaved man from a neighbouring farm, whose owner forbade it. She was made to marry an older man, Thomas, and had five children; her first, James, died in childhood.

New York's gradual emancipation law set 4 July 1827 as the day the older enslaved people would go free. Dumont promised to free her a year early, then broke his word. So in 1826 she walked away, by daylight, carrying her baby daughter Sophia. Isaac and Maria Van Wagenen of New Paltz took her in and paid Dumont twenty dollars for the rest of her year.
The case for Peter

Then she learned that Dumont had sold her five-year-old son, Peter, out of the state, to a man in Alabama. New York law forbade it. With the Van Wagenens' help she took the case to court, and in 1828 she won: Peter was brought back to New York. The court papers were rediscovered in the New York State Archives only a few years ago. She is often described as the first Black woman to win a case against a white man; sources word that claim in different ways, so it is not made here.

In 1829 she and Peter moved to New York City, where she worked as a housekeeper. In 1839 Peter took a job on a whaling ship. When the ship came back in 1842 he was not on it, and she never heard from him again.
Sojourner Truth

In 1843, saying God had called her to testify, she took the name Sojourner Truth and set out to preach against slavery. In 1844 she joined a community of abolitionists at Northampton, Massachusetts, where she met William Lloyd Garrison and Frederick Douglass. She could not write, so she dictated her life to a friend, Olive Gilbert, and in 1850 Garrison published it as the Narrative of Sojourner Truth. That year she spoke at the first national women's rights convention, in Worcester.
Akron, 1851

In May 1851 she spoke at a women's rights convention in Akron, Ohio. The speech everyone knows as "Ain't I a Woman?" is also her most disputed. The version quoted today was published by Frances Gage in 1863, twelve years later, in a dialect of the Southern plantations that Truth, who grew up speaking Dutch in New York, never had. A report printed by Marius Robinson a month after the speech does not contain the phrase at all. The National Park Service presents the famous text as disputed, and so do we.
Selling the shadow

She paid for her work by selling small portrait cards of herself, printed with the words "I sell the shadow to support the substance": the shadow was the photograph, the substance was herself. During the Civil War she recruited Black soldiers; a grandson served in the 54th Massachusetts. In 1864, working for freed people in Washington, she met Abraham Lincoln, and she rode the city's streetcars to force their desegregation. From 1870 she petitioned, without success, for land grants for the formerly enslaved, and met President Grant; in 1872 she went to vote in Battle Creek, Michigan, and was turned away.
Sojourner Truth died at her home in Battle Creek on 26 November 1883. In 2009 she became the first Black woman honoured with a bust in the United States Capitol.
